title: What is a CTE (`WITH ...`), how does it improve readability over nested subqueries, and how does a recursive CTE (`WITH RECURSIVE`) traverse hierarchical data (org charts, trees, graphs) with an anchor + recursive member?

s1_definition.profdef: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named, temporary result set defined with a `WITH` clause that exists for the duration of a single query. It improves readability by letting you name and reuse intermediate results instead of deeply nesting subqueries. A recursive CTE (`WITH RECURSIVE`) has an anchor member that produces the starting rows and a recursive member that repeatedly joins back to the CTE itself, used to walk hierarchical data like org charts and trees until no new rows are produced.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine solving a complex report at National Bank of India in steps. Instead of cramming every step inside nested brackets, a CTE lets you name each step like "first, let me define high_value_accounts" and then use that name later, reading top to bottom like a recipe. A recursive CTE is like tracing a reporting chain: start with the branch manager (the anchor), then find everyone who reports to them, then everyone who reports to those people, and keep going down the tree until nobody is left.
s1_definition.oneliner: A CTE is a named `WITH` block that makes queries read top-to-bottom like steps, and a recursive CTE walks hierarchies with an anchor row plus a self-referencing recursive step.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named, temporary result set defined with a `WITH` clause that exists for the duration of a single query. It improves readability by letting you name and reuse intermediate results instead of deeply nesting subqueries. A recursive CTE (`WITH RECURSIVE`) has an anchor member that produces the starting rows and a recursive member that repeatedly joins back to the CTE itself, used to walk hierarchical data like org charts and trees until no new rows are produced.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine solving a complex report at National Bank of India in steps. Instead of cramming every step inside nested brackets, a CTE lets you name each step like "first, let me define high_value_accounts" and then use that name later, reading top to bottom like a recipe. A recursive CTE is like tracing a reporting chain: start with the branch manager (the anchor), then find everyone who reports to them, then everyone who reports to those people, and keep going down the tree until nobody is left.

**One line to remember:** A CTE is a named `WITH` block that makes queries read top-to-bottom like steps, and a recursive CTE walks hierarchies with an anchor row plus a self-referencing recursive step.

sections.s2_technical:
A CTE is introduced with `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)` and then referenced by that name in the main query, exactly as if it were a table. You can define several CTEs separated by commas, and later CTEs can reference earlier ones, which lets you build a pipeline of named steps. Compared with nested subqueries, the benefit is readability: a three-level nested subquery reads inside-out and is hard to follow, whereas three chained CTEs read top-to-bottom as named stages, each testable on its own. A CTE also lets you reference the same intermediate result more than once by name instead of repeating the subquery.

A recursive CTE uses `WITH RECURSIVE name AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive_member)`. The anchor member runs once and seeds the result with the starting rows, for example the top manager whose manager id is NULL. The recursive member then references `name` itself and joins it to the base table to find the next level, for example employees whose manager is in the current result. The engine repeats the recursive member, each iteration feeding the newly produced rows back in, until an iteration produces no new rows, at which point recursion stops. The `UNION ALL` accumulates all levels.

Recursive CTEs are how you traverse trees and graphs in pure SQL: org charts (who reports to whom, at any depth), category hierarchies, bill-of-materials, and account-linkage graphs. You typically carry a depth counter and a path so you can control depth and detect cycles — graphs with loops need a cycle guard, otherwise recursion never terminates, which many engines support with a `CYCLE` clause or by checking the accumulated path. A senior nuance is that `UNION ALL` is used (not `UNION`) for performance because de-duplication each iteration is costly, and cycle protection is handled explicitly instead. Another nuance is that some engines materialize a CTE (compute it once) while others inline it, which affects performance, so for hot queries you check the plan.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a reporting query that first finds high-value accounts, then finds their large transactions, then summarizes by branch. Written as nested subqueries it was an unreadable three-level nest that nobody wanted to touch. Rewriting it as named CTEs made each stage a clear, named step.

Problem 2 — The HR system stores the branch staff as an org chart: each employee row has a manager id pointing to another employee, and the branch manager's manager id is NULL. The bank wants the full reporting tree under the branch manager, at any depth. This is a classic recursive CTE: anchor on the branch manager, then repeatedly find direct reports.

Our mini-project builds an `OrgHierarchyService` that walks the employee reporting tree using the anchor-plus-recursive-member pattern in memory, carrying a depth level, and a small CTE-pipeline example for the high-value report. It includes an `Employee` model, a repository, the service, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four employees. Rajesh (E1) is the branch manager with no manager. Priya (E2) and Amit (E3) report to Rajesh. Neha (E4) reports to Priya.

Step 1 — The anchor member runs once. It finds every employee whose manager id is NULL, which is just Rajesh (E1), and assigns him level 1. The result starts as [Rajesh@1] and the frontier is [Rajesh].

Step 2 — The first recursive iteration takes the frontier (Rajesh) and finds everyone whose manager id equals an employee in the frontier. Priya and Amit both report to E1, so they are produced at level 2. The result grows to [Rajesh@1, Priya@2, Amit@2] and the new frontier becomes [Priya, Amit].

Step 3 — The second recursive iteration takes the frontier (Priya, Amit) and finds their reports. Neha reports to Priya (E2), so she is produced at level 3. Amit has no reports. The result grows to include Neha@3 and the new frontier is [Neha].

Step 4 — The third iteration takes the frontier (Neha) and looks for her reports. Nobody reports to Neha, so no new rows are produced. The frontier is now empty, so recursion stops. This is exactly how a recursive CTE terminates — when an iteration adds nothing.

Step 5 — The accumulated tree is returned with each employee's level, showing the full hierarchy under the branch manager.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] === Recursive CTE: full org tree (anchor + recursive member) ===
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] lvl1 Rajesh Kumar (E1)
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] lvl2   Priya Sharma (E2)
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] lvl2   Amit Verma (E3)
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] lvl3     Neha Gupta (E4)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  employees: E1(mgr=NULL) E2(mgr=E1) E3(mgr=E1) E4(mgr=E2)
    │
    ▼  ANCHOR: WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  [ E1 Rajesh lvl1 ]                        frontier = {E1}
    │
    ▼  RECURSIVE iter 1: e.manager_id = org.emp_id
  [ E2 Priya lvl2, E3 Amit lvl2 ]           frontier = {E2,E3}
    │
    ▼  RECURSIVE iter 2
  [ E4 Neha lvl3 ]                          frontier = {E4}
    │
    ▼  RECURSIVE iter 3 → no new rows → STOP
  UNION ALL accumulation:
    E1(1) → E2(2), E3(2) → E4(3)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Common Table Expression, or CTE, is a named temporary result set defined with a `WITH` clause that lives only for the duration of a single query. You write `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)` and then reference that name in the main query as if it were a table, and you can chain several CTEs where later ones build on earlier ones. The readability win over nested subqueries is real: a deeply nested subquery reads inside-out and is painful to follow, whereas chained CTEs read top-to-bottom as clearly named stages, each one testable on its own. At the National Bank of India we rewrote an unreadable three-level nested reporting query into three named CTEs — high-value accounts, their large transactions, and a branch summary — and it became something the whole team could maintain.

A recursive CTE, written `WITH RECURSIVE`, is how you traverse hierarchical data in pure SQL. It has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`: an anchor member that runs once to produce the starting rows, and a recursive member that references the CTE itself to find the next level. For our branch org chart, the anchor selects the branch manager whose manager id is NULL, and the recursive member repeatedly finds employees whose manager is already in the result, carrying a level counter. The engine keeps applying the recursive member, feeding each new batch of rows back in, until an iteration produces no new rows, at which point recursion stops naturally.

This pattern handles org charts, category trees, bills of materials, and account-linkage graphs. A few senior points I always mention: we use `UNION ALL` rather than `UNION` because de-duplicating every iteration is expensive, and we carry a depth counter and an accumulated path so we can limit depth and detect cycles, since a graph with a loop would otherwise recurse forever — many engines offer a `CYCLE` clause for exactly this. I also note that whether an engine materializes or inlines a CTE affects performance, so for a hot query I check the execution plan and index the join column, which for a hierarchy is the manager id. The line I always state is that a CTE is a named `WITH` block that makes queries read top-to-bottom like steps, and a recursive CTE walks hierarchies with an anchor row plus a self-referencing recursive step.

keyPoints: Correlated subquery: references outer query — runs per row
CTE (WITH clause): named temporary result set
Recursive CTE: hierarchical queries (org chart, tree structures)
